title: Conversations about academic authorship need to be transparent
summary: Madeleine Pownall and Mary Hausfeld call for research teams to be more explicit, equitable, and reflective about how they assign scholarly credit
full_text:
Authorship carries enormous professional power within academia.

In many disciplines, decisions about who appears first, last, or in middle authorship positions shape hiring opportunities, promotion, funding success, and professional visibility.

For early career researchers especially, authorship can determine access to future academic careers. Despite this, authorship discussions are often informal, delayed, or avoided entirely, which leaves room for misunderstanding, inequity, and conflict.

Speaking out

Current approaches to authorship frequently rely upon individuals speaking out if they believe decisions are unfair.

However, this assumes that all researchers occupy equal positions of power within research teams, which is rarely the case. Hierarchies relating to seniority, gender, race, disability, institutional prestige, contract precarity, and other forms of privilege shape who feels able to challenge decisions and whose contributions are most readily recognised (see the Academic Wheel of Privilege). In this context, expecting junior or marginalised researchers to independently contest authorship decisions places an unfair burden on those with the least institutional power.

The challenge is that most authorship disputes are typically not the result of deliberate misconduct.

More often, they emerge because collaborators simply have different assumptions about what kinds of work should be recognised and when those conversations should take place. One researcher may view conceptualising the project as the defining contribution, another may place greater value on data collection or manuscript drafting, while yet another assumes that project management or supervision should carry significant weight.

Unless these expectations are made explicit, collaborators can work on the same project while holding fundamentally different ideas about how credit will ultimately be allocated.

Tracing a solution

This issue is becoming more pressing as research itself changes. Collaborative, interdisciplinary, international or “big team science” projects are increasingly the norm, involving larger teams and more diverse forms of expertise. Alongside traditional scholarly activities sit forms of labour that often receive less recognition, including project management, stakeholder engagement, mentoring, administrative coordination and community partnership.

Existing authorship guidelines help define who qualifies for authorship, but they do little to facilitate the conversations that teams need in order to reach shared expectations.

There could be a simple way to fix this. For example, a “tool” that we are loosely terming TRACE: Transparent Review of Authorship Contribution Expectations could be a place to start.

TRACE is, in theory, an easy-to-implement, scalable, and customisable tool designed to facilitate earlier, more transparent, more reflective, and ideally more equitable conversations about authorship within academic research teams.

TRACE asks collaborators to independently and anonymously reflect on anticipated contributions, expectations around authorship order, and areas of labour they believe risk being overlooked.

Rather than producing an algorithm for determining authorship, the process is designed to reveal where expectations are mismatched so that discussions can happen early, before disagreements become conflicts. Therefore, instead of relying on spontaneous conversations about authorship, which can often be uncomfortable, or retrospective conflict resolution, the TRACE process provides collaborators with a structured opportunity to independently reflect on contributions, expectations, and authorship. This allows teams to surface misperceptions of authorship order expectations in a transparent way.

We have developed two versions of the tool, one intended for early conversations as projects are just beginning, the other for later conversations, such as just before submitting to a journal, which are available as Qualtrics templates here.

This approach may also help address longstanding inequities in academic recognition. Research consistently demonstrates that women and marginalised scholars are more likely to have their labour overlooked, minimised, or attributed to senior colleagues. Transparent systems of expectation-sharing can encourage accountability and create opportunities to examine whether recognition aligns fairly with contribution.

Given the immense power attached to authorship within academia, we argue that research teams should adopt more explicit, equitable, and reflective approaches to determining scholarly credit. TRACE is one place to start.

title: From access to graduate success: the next phase of social mobility

The post From access to graduate success: the next phase of social mobility appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Professor Sir Nishan Canagarajah, President and Vice-Chancellor of the University of Leicester and Martin Edmondson, Chief Executive of the Graduate Futures Institute.

Access is not enough

Britain has made real progress in widening access to higher education. More people, from more backgrounds, now have the chance to benefit from university than in previous generations. But access to university is no longer the whole social mobility story.

Disadvantage can persist through higher education and into employment. The continuing challenge is to ensure graduates from every background can access meaningful work, build confidence and secure opportunity.

This challenge is at the heart of From Access to Graduate Success: The Next Phase of Social Mobility, a new report launched by the Graduate Futures Institute, in partnership with the University of Leicester.

The report draws on 288 professionals working across 107 UK higher education providers, alongside 47 institutional perspectives. Of survey respondents:

97 per cent agreed that students from under-represented groups face employment disadvantage compared with their peers;

96 per cent said work-related learning is essential or very important in reducing that disadvantage; and

69 per cent believed some under-represented groups are at greater risk of being left behind as AI tools reshape the labour market.

These findings do not point to a lack of talent or excess of graduates. They indicate unequal access to what helps people progress: professional networks, paid experience, recruitment knowledge, financial flexibility, confidence and careers support.

A shared jobs challenge

Universities UK’s Future Jobs Roadmap makes the economic case clearly: the future economy will need more graduates, and employers need stronger links with universities to access the skills required for growth.

But the transition into work is still uneven. Graduates are more likely than non-graduates to be in education or employment and tend to move into work more quickly, yet too many still face difficult starts, especially those from under-represented groups or weaker regional labour markets.

If Britain wants stronger growth, higher productivity and a fairer labour market, graduate opportunity must become a shared national priority. Universities can prepare students, but employers, local authorities and government can help turn that preparation into real opportunity.

Higher education’s public promise

Higher education matters for many reasons: intellectual growth, civic participation, cultural enrichment and economic benefit. But for students and families, the prospect of a better career is a central part of its public promise.

That does not reduce university to a single employment metric; it recognises that fair access to graduate careers is now an important test of whether higher education is delivering on social mobility.

We should be honest about what is at stake. Graduate opportunity affects who gets to build influence, enter the professions, lead institutions and shape society. Research by LSE in Born to Rule: the making and remaking of the British elite found that “there is less movement at the top than we think”, with those born into the top one per cent almost as likely to enter the elite today as they were 125 years ago.

If we want our institutions, professions and public life to better reflect the talent of the whole population, universities, government and employers must work together to remove the barriers that prevent capable graduates from progressing.

The recent creation of the Class Unit in the Office for Equality and Opportunity should sharpen the national focus on this agenda. It speaks directly to this report’s central challenge: talent is not lacking, but routes into good work are still too often shaped by networks, assumptions and uneven access to opportunity.

Putting this into practice

For universities, the response must be practical and strategic. Employability support should reach students who cannot easily access optional activities. Targeted guidance, mentoring and specialist provision should be protected where barriers are greatest, and work-related learning should be embedded in the curriculum.

At Leicester, we have been putting this into practice by designing opportunity directly into the student experience. Every student has access to at least 100 hours of work-related learning as part of their degree, ensuring they graduate with real-world experience, confidence and the skills employers value. Through our collaboration with Microsoft, which gives every student full and equitable access to Microsoft’s Copilot AI tools, and by embedding use of AI across our teaching and assessment, we are helping students develop the digital and AI capabilities that will increasingly shape graduate careers.

The sector already knows much about effective practice, yet financial pressure is reconfiguring provision. Many of the activities respondents value most, including one-to-one guidance, specialist roles and bursary-backed experience, are also among those being reduced. This risks compounding the challenges faced by students who most need support. Digital and AI-enabled services can extend reach, but they complement human support rather than substitute for it.

Universities cannot do this alone. Employers should create more paid, accessible entry routes, backed by inclusive recruitment, induction and progression. Government should make it easier and less risky for employers, particularly SMEs, to recruit new graduates in weaker regional labour markets. Local authorities and civic partners should help connect talent, transport, employers and place-based growth.

From participation to opportunity

Widening access to university has been one of the major social mobility achievements of recent decades. The next phase is to widen access to graduate success.

We must support every student to access the skills, confidence, networks and experiences needed to succeed after graduation. Anything less risks asking students to reach the door of opportunity, only to find that others still hold the key.

title: How Apprenticeships Can Help Colleges Access Workforce Pell
summary:
How Apprenticeships Can Help Colleges Access Workforce Pell Olivia.sanchez Tue, 09/22/2026 - 03:00 AM Registered apprenticeships that include some instruction from a college automatically qualify as “in-demand,” giving institutions a potential fast track to Workforce Pell. Byline(s) Olivia Sanchez How Apprenticeships Can Help Colleges Access Workforce Pell
Olivia.sanchez Tue, 09/22/2026 - 03:00 AM

Registered apprenticeships that include some instruction from a college automatically qualify as “in-demand,” giving institutions a potential fast track to Workforce Pell.

Byline(s)
Olivia Sanchez
full_text:
The promise of Workforce Pell could expand opportunities for Americans seeking short-term career training—and, if it manifests, the opportunities will extend to thousands of people who enroll in certain registered apprenticeships, according to new guidance from the Department of Labor.

Although apprenticeships weren’t mentioned by name in the law passed by Congress—which expanded the types of programs low-income students can spend Pell dollars on—the Department of Education included several provisions in the regulations that make it possible for many registered apprenticeship programs to qualify. President Donald Trump is a proponent of apprenticeships—his administration has announced a goal of getting one million people into apprenticeship programs.

Registered apprenticeships must include related technical instruction, and Labor said in the guidance that Workforce Pell can help the sponsor cover expenses related to that component.

While the policy allowing for Workforce Pell went into effect July 1, only five programs have been approved to date. The slow rollout is in part because of the strict eligibility criteria and role that state leaders play in determining which types of programs can qualify.

Joe E. Ross, president of the apprenticeship-degree provider Reach University, said the new guidance will help apprenticeship programs circumvent several of the main challenges that colleges might encounter while trying to stand up Workforce Pell programs.

“I think what people are feeling right now is that Workforce Pell looks hard and complicated,” Ross said. “What the Department of Labor has done is created a way for it to be easier by leveraging the apprenticeship system as kind of a fast track for Workforce Pell.”

According to the DOL guidance, released last week, programs that partner with registered apprenticeships can automatically qualify as “high-skill, high-wage or in-demand” if part of the instruction comes from a college—something that institutions would otherwise have to prove to state leaders. Those programs can then outsource up to 49 percent of instruction to an outside entity, like a labor union, employer or another training provider, compared to the maximum 25 percent for nonapprenticeship Workforce Pell programs. The guidance also makes clear that programs that include more than 15 weeks of instruction can still be eligible, as long as those weeks are broken up by on-the-job learning.

The DOL encouraged registered apprenticeship providers to consider partnering with colleges for the training, to break up instructional time in longer programs and to consider what funding streams could be combined with Workforce Pell to cover the full cost of attendance for apprentices.

Although the guidance just came out, Ross said he expects the clarity it provides will lead to an increase in institutions applying for Workforce Pell approval.

Deborah Kobes, a senior fellow at the nonpartisan Urban Institute, said that while most registered apprenticeships are offered by labor unions or employers, community colleges have often partnered with apprenticeship programs to handle parts of the instruction.

She said that by including registered apprenticeships in Workforce Pell, the federal government is incentivizing more colleges to begin offering apprenticeship programs or expand their existing offerings.

“Apprenticeships are in an interesting space because they’re not a traditional higher ed program, so in that sense they align with the sort of workforce goals of having more high-quality training opportunities,” Kobes said. “But they’re different from most Workforce Pell programs because they are designed as long-term programs.”

She said that much of the instruction in apprenticeship programs already comes from industry experts, and allowing programs to qualify even if they outsource 49 percent of their content is a way of recognizing that.

“Being a sponsor at the community college is a really great way to engage small and medium-sized businesses in apprenticeship. Because, as a small employer, if you only have one or two apprentices, you might not have that scale that you need to really deliver the related instructions,” Kobes said. However, “if a community college takes the lead on delivering an apprenticeship, they can aggregate the interest of local employers.”

Mark D’Amico, a professor of higher education at the University of North Caroline Charlotte, said that registered apprenticeships will still have to meet all the other qualifications in order to be approved for Workforce Pell, such as offering academic credit and meeting certain thresholds for completion rates and job-placement rates.

“The Workforce Pell–approved program is still through a Title IV–eligible institution,” D’Amico said, referring to the section of federal law that authorizes student aid. “For students and apprentices, they’re going to be receiving higher education through the higher ed institution with all of the protections that would be a part of approval for a nonapprenticeship Workforce Pell program.”

title: The Way(s) Forward on Measuring Learning
summary:
The Way(s) Forward on Measuring Learning Doug Lederman Tue, 09/22/2026 - 03:00 AM Higher education must prove to the public that students are ready for work and life. Here’s how we might do that. Byline(s) Doug Lederman The Way(s) Forward on Measuring Learning
Doug Lederman Tue, 09/22/2026 - 03:00 AM

Higher education must prove to the public that students are ready for work and life. Here’s how we might do that.

Byline(s)
Doug Lederman
full_text:
This is the third and last piece in my miniseries on measuring learning. Thanks for sticking it out; you’re almost there. Buckle up: This one’s long.

Three weeks ago in this space I explained why I believe colleges and universities must prove they’re actually helping students develop the capabilities, skills and habits of mind they say they are.

Last week I described how we got here—to the point that the public increasingly questions the value of degrees and of going to college at all, in part because they doubt learning is occurring. Confidence in higher education’s internal evaluations based on faculty judgment and grades has eroded, and external accountability systems have done as much damage as good.

Now comes the really hard part: suggesting how we might certify that students are ready, to prove to the public that postsecondary education is delivering what it promises, at a time when the emergence of artificial intelligence is reshaping how we work and live.

As a journalist for 40 years, finding solutions wasn’t my responsibility. I mostly pointed out others’ problems and nagged them to fix them. Now I feel an obligation to be more constructive given my current role as … wait, what am I? Consultant? Talking head? Believer in higher education yet healthy skeptic of how it’s performing?

Still, I venture into this space humbly. I’ve never designed a curriculum. Or taught a group of students. Or tried to measure learning. I know what I don’t know.

What I do know is that higher education has a credibility problem. Too many people now doubt whether the time and money they expend pursuing a credential at American colleges and universities are worth it, and whether the credentials they receive will be valued by employers.

Measuring learning won’t address the credibility gap by itself; we also need to make postsecondary education more affordable, improve postcollege earnings and other outcomes, and, yes, tell our story better so Americans remember that higher education actually does a lot of important things well.

But documenting whether and how much learning is happening is essential to the “value” argument; as I wrote a few weeks ago, “it’s hard to persuade people that your primary ‘product’ is worth paying for when you can’t prove they’re actually getting it.”

So how might we reach the “holy grail” of truly measuring student learning?

Step 1: What Do We Want to Measure?

The question of “what is college for?” has many answers, and no single valid response. But many of the arguments we have—is it for career preparation or broad knowledge? Personal growth or earnings potential?—are binary to the point of banality.

Yes, colleges in different sectors have varying missions, and institutions that specialize in fields with licensure exams (think nursing, law and engineering) have external, structured targets for student knowledge and development.

But if you zero in specifically on what colleges promise to their undergraduate students (as opposed to their local communities through business development, or to society at large through research), they look way more alike than different.

Take the core educational competencies that, say, the Virginia Community College System wants its students to develop, and compare them to Michigan Technological University’s 12 “essential abilities”; Stanford University’s “ways of thinking, ways of doing”; and Carleton College’s “higher-order thinking skills.”

Given the differences in these institutions’ missions, it’s not surprising to see modest variation in the language they use to describe what they are striving for in educating learners. But all of them identify capacities such as critical (or analytical) thinking, communication, quantitative reasoning, ethical or civic capacity, breadth (or depth) of knowledge, and working with others (or across difference).

Widening the prism, we’ve seen several larger past efforts to define the competencies and skills of a college-educated person. The Liberal Education and America’s Promise initiative’s Essential Learning Outcomes Framework from the American Association of Colleges and Universities morphed into the VALUE rubrics, and Lumina Foundation’s 2011 Degree Qualifications Profile sought to gauge what learners should know and be able to do by the time they’ve attained an associate, bachelor’s or master’s degree, regardless of field.

These frameworks offer a useful starting point to show we could develop a common definition of the capabilities, knowledge, skills and habits of mind that learners should acquire with the help of an educational experience.

Both are at least a decade old, though, so they probably need revisiting to account for the emergence of AI, which is scrambling our understanding of work and what current and future workers (and human beings) need to know and be able to do.

Let’s throw into the mix, then, an emerging set of frameworks around what people outside higher education (and a few inside it) call durable skills: the capabilities and competencies employers believe will remain relevant in the face of whatever technological advancement or other massive societal changes are visited upon us.

These models come from organizations at the intersection of education and employment, like the National Association of Colleges and Employers, America Succeeds, the World Economic Forum, and the Education Design Lab. The Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching is developing its own right now.

These frameworks overlap substantially with the ones developed by AAC&U and Lumina; they all include some version of critical thinking and reasoning, problem-solving, ethical judgment, communication and collaboration.

But they diverge in other ways: Those developed with higher education in mind prioritize deep knowledge of a discipline, which doesn’t appear in the work-focused systems. The durable-skills frameworks, meanwhile, emphasize the importance of personal traits like self-management, resilience and capacity for growth, which are largely absent from the Degree Qualifications Profile and VALUE frameworks.

Picture a process, then, in which we convened a group of people who approach post–high school learning from varying perspectives: faculty members from multiple fields, assessment experts, administrators from an array of colleges and universities, employers, researchers on the future of work, high school educators, and maybe a few actual learners.

Their goal: coalesce around a forward-looking, detailed framework for what a person “educated” after high school ought to know and be able to do to work and function effectively in society. (I’d picture it having 10 or fewer high-level capacities, cascading to a larger number of subskills. Broad enough to capture what’s important, targeted enough to be meaningful and to give us a snowball’s chance of being measurable.)

The diversity of the group would be essential because of a core tension underlying this whole conversation: Who judges what learning is and whether it’s happening? For centuries it was largely left to colleges’ faculty, but the employers who hire students and the learners themselves clearly have a stake, too.

That’s why we must strive for a consensus among them on any attempt to define goals for what colleges and universities should be shooting for in educating learners, and ultimately what we should be measuring against.

Step 2: A Question Before ‘How’?

Some wise souls have warned me that reaching any kind of collective agreement on what a college-educated person should know and be able to do is a fool’s errand. I take that seriously, as I don’t want to be Don Quixote at this stage of my career. Humor me for a moment and assume that the process I just described results in a blueprint that is palatable to professors of all stripes, corporate HR managers and parents and students alike. (A boy can dream.)

Before we get to the really tricky dilemma of how we might measure whether learners are reaching the goals we set, one key question demands consideration. (People like John Warner have raised others, not all of which I can get to in this column.)

Proficiency or growth? An age-old debate in education research is whether it’s more important to assess whether learners know or can do something (proficiency or competency) or how much more they know or can do than they did before (growth).

The debate particularly rages in accountability circles (especially in K–12) because measuring proficiency sets a clear common standard but doesn’t account for differences in where students started, so it benefits schools (or colleges) dominated by well-prepared students (and hurts those that serve many disadvantaged learners).

For the purposes of this column, the question is whether we’d strive for some measure of competence (upon completion of a degree program or curriculum, does Jane know x and can Johnny do y, and how well?) or seek some kind of value-added measure that shows how much better (or worse) Alex and Pat are at knowing or doing things than they were when they appeared at our door.

Here’s why that matters. A competence measure would tell us most of what we need to know for the sake of learners themselves: Are they ready for what comes next in work and life? It could certainly tell us something about the performance of colleges and universities, too: Are Monumental State U or Cozy College generally delivering on the commitments they make to learners?

A value-added measure would answer those questions and provide something else, too: a sense of how much the college or university journey itself has helped develop its learners. By gauging what learners know and can do at the beginning and end of an educational experience (or at points along the way), we’d also get a sense of which institutions do the most with the students they enroll, regardless of their previous preparation and background.

The latter appeals to me personally, because one of my stubborn beliefs is that the public regularly assumes that the “best” colleges, where you learn the most, are the highly selective and wealthy ones that frequently filter out the students who need the most support. I’ve argued before that I’d bet that students at Fill-in-the-Blank Community College learn and grow more during their time there than do their peers at Highfalutin University in the fancy suburb next door.

A value-added learning tool would prove me right (or wrong), so I’m drawn to that. It would also be more useful from an accountability standpoint, since it would create a more level playing field for judging the contributions of the institutions themselves.

But creating a system that measured growth would also be much more complicated and expensive, because it would require evaluation at multiple points. And ultimately, what matters most to me (given my primary focus on restoring public confidence in higher ed’s value, rather than on accountability or internal improvement) is whether learners are prepared or not for what comes next. So I’d favor a measurement mechanism focused on competency, at least as a start.

Step 3: How Might We Measure?

I’m going to spend a lot less time on this final section than I originally planned, for two reasons: (1) As I worked on this set of columns, I’ve realized that the most important task by far is defining (and reaching consensus on) what we want today’s and tomorrow’s learners to know and be able to do. So many good things would flow from doing that that how we measure it might matter less. And (2) the how is really hard, and I honestly have few answers for that. But I’ll try anyway.

The short version is this: Once we’ve developed a common framework for what students know and can do, there are two likely options—a capstone test/exit exam, or a method of evaluating authentic student work against the framework.

The Test: The prospect that some kind of examination could accurately measure whether students have the capabilities, skills, knowledge and habits of mind is enticing. It would satisfy those who favor a significant level of cross-institutional “objectivity” over the subjective judgment that plagues our historical approach: a diploma purportedly certifying learning based on faculty judgment (grades) on a set of completed assignments and assessments, plus time spent in the hallowed halls (credit hours).

I suspect that if we poured a ton of money and energy into the effort, we could improve on previous efforts like the GRE and the Collegiate Learning Assessment (see last column) and end up with something that might satisfy psychometricians and politicians. Concerns about the price tag and how you’d incentivize learners to take the test seriously might be hard to overcome.

Most faculty members would hate it for more reasons than I can list, and they’d be right about some of them.

Would it be worth trying? Heck yes. Am I optimistic that it would work, or that it would be the best option? No.

Portfolios of student work: If the goal is to develop a mechanism for evaluating and certifying learning in a way that is persuasive to the public yet acceptable to faculty members, it’s much more likely to come from analysis of authentic student work than from some external examination. (There are more and less justifiable reasons that many professors dismiss assessment of learning, but faculty worries that students would focus on an externally derived tool at the expense of their actual course of study are legit.)

The use of electronic portfolios as an assessment tool in higher education emerged in part as a response to testing because they allowed for evaluation of actual student work in a low-stakes environment tied to material professors valued. They also build in students’ reflection on their own growth in a way that most exams don’t.

Picture an approach where the set of capacities developed by my learning supergroup would be turned into a rubric against which a collection of authentic student work was judged. (If this sounds like how AAC&U’s VALUE system works, yes, same ballpark. Some competency-based education approaches work this way, too.)

I’m drawn to the competency-based approach of gauging learners’ levels of proficiency (e.g., novice, developing, proficient, distinguished) rather than a grade or numerical rating for each competency. Whether that would be specific enough to satisfy all the audiences this whole process might need to serve is a question for another day.

Inertia and faculty distrust of common rubrics substituted for their own personal judgment are two major (and I’d say flawed) reasons why competency-based approaches haven’t taken hold in the way advocates hoped. The convoluted regulatory environment around federal financial aid has probably been the biggest impediment.

But another, very legitimate practical one is the cost and labor intensity of actually scoring student work. Creating an infrastructure to collect, tag and organize all the artifacts that learners produce—assessments, papers, videos, oral presentations, team projects, statistical models, musical scores—and then training and compensating faculty to judge and score the student work against a rubric is complicated and expensive. Nobody has had the incentive to invest in doing so at scale so far.

I’d argue that we arguably have the incentive now—you know, to maybe prove that going to college is worth it, to save the industry all those professors work in?

But this is also where technology, which may be our collective downfall, may also be an ally.

What if we could marshal the power of artificial intelligence to effectively (over time, with an enormous amount of training and human oversight) grade authentic student work conceived and assigned by real, live faculty members against the competency rubric we’ve developed?

I’m way outside my depth here, but smart people like Eddie Watson and Kate McConnell at AAC&U and Tim Knowles and Brooke Stafford-Brizard at Carnegie are already thinking about this, as I’m sure are others I haven’t spoken to. Technology companies are making lots of promises, too, and I take every single one of them with tablets, not grains, of salt.

The End, for Now

I’m running out of steam here (as are you, if you’ve made it this far, probably), so I’ll conclude with this.

If the grand vision I’ve just laid out came to pass, the next few steps would involve using the new information we’ve gleaned (about how well students are developing the capabilities we want them to have) to embrace more of the curricular and teaching approaches that research has shown to work best.

We’d make the information publicly available to help upend a student decision-making process that too often is based on colleges’ reputation, wealth, marketing budgets and the like.

We’d develop better navigation systems to match learners and potential employers based on the documented strengths and weaknesses they exhibit on the durable capacities we’ve agreed on.

I’m sure I’ve tried to do too much in this series of articles, and yet not enough, too.

Mainly what I want is to try to stimulate more and better thinking about what we want college-level learning to be in this important, possibly existential moment, and how we might reassure those who’ve lost faith in us that we can, and want to, be better.

title: Lack of child care costs families, business and taxpayers $122 billion: study
summary: 1 in 4 parents has had to quit a job because of child care problems, according to the study.
full_text:
When parents can't find adequate child care, they might miss work, get fired or choose to leave the workforce entirely — all of which not only affects how much money families earn, but costs businesses and taxpayers. And the situation has gotten worse in recent years. According to the study from ReadyNation, the economy is losing out on an estimated $122 billion a year.

The report found that not having child care — or enough child care — costs individual parents more than $5,500 a year, or more than $78 billion in total. And businesses lose $1,640 on average for each working parent due to lost revenue and hiring costs because of insufficient child care, totaling $23 billion annually. And the government loses, too — about $21 billion in lost income and sales tax revenues a year, or $1,470 less per working parent because parents without enough child care earn less and therefore consume less in their communities.

"We did this four years ago, and it's bad. We did it now and it's worse, and absent any real policy solutions to the child care crisis, this is just going to go on and on," said Sandra Bishop, chief research officer for the bipartisan nonprofit Council for a Stronger America, which includes three organizations including ReadyNation.

The $122 billion in losses is more than double what the same study found in 2018, when the economy lost out on $57 billion a year due to the child care crisis.

"We found that the impacts were more widespread and more severe," Bishop said of the latest results. "More parents were reporting the negative impacts on their work and in some cases dramatically – I think it was twice as many people fired, more people quitting."

She also called the estimated losses a "gross underestimate" because it only looked at the challenges for parents with children under three while parents face issues with childcare well beyond that age group.

The report found 85% of primary caregivers said the challenges with child care are cutting into their work hours or productivity, including 64% saying it's made them late to work in the past three months. A majority — 58% — reported missing a full day of work; while 53% reported being distracted at work. Child care has even affected how much or if parents work: 33% have switched from full time to part time, while 26% of parents reported quitting a job due to child care problems and another 23% reported getting fired.

This comes as the United States is facing an ongoing labor shortage. At the end of last year, there were more than 11 million job openings. Quitting rates remain above pre-pandemic levels. For many businesses, finding qualified workers remains one of the greatest challenges.

For the manufacturing company Contec Inc. in Spartanburg, South Carolina, a worker shortage has been an ongoing challenge – and the company has lost workers due to child care.

"If they need to go to a different shift which would enable them to take care of their children when nobody's home, we'll certainly make those accommodations," said founder and CEO Jack McBride, of the challenges. He said they've also told people who have had to leave due to child care they will hold their positions should they find the help because they need workers so badly.

Demand for the company's cleaning and disinfectant products remained high throughout the pandemic. Having enough workers to meet that demand would mean more sales — but right now, they're paying their existing workers "a ton" of overtime instead. McBride welcomed going in with other businesses to provide child care, but the cost-benefit for onsite care doesn't make sense for his company alone.

What Contec Inc. does have in the works is the implementation of three months childcare leave for both parents starting this summer, which will help new parents bond while covering the early expenses. He's also been working in Spartanburg to educate on the importance of early childhood education.

As families struggle with childcare costs – a growing number of employers have begun to provide pre-tax dependent care spending accounts. Last year saw a 6% increase from 2021, according to the human resources association World at Work which surveyed more than 800 organizations of all sizes. However, most don't contribute directly to such accounts, so the cost to companies is fairly low. The tax savings from such accounts can be a big help, but they were capped at $5,000 in 2022, below the median cost of child care.

A growing number – 49% – offer employees child care resources and referrals, according to World at Work data. Only 10% of offered on-site or near-site child care centers – up from 7% in 2016, but down from the 12% peak in 2020 and 2021. Only 9% offer subsidies or discounts – which was virtually unchanged since 2016.

For smaller businesses, workers having child care is an even greater challenge. One survey found over half of small-business owners said their employees had to deal with child care challenges during the pandemic, and 80% of small business owners supported congressional intervention to increase access to affordable care.

Across the country, the number of child care centers and home-based care options have not returned to where they were before the pandemic. And federal money aimed at stabilizing the system at the height of the pandemic will start to expire later this year. Experts and business owners alike are concerned it will result in more workers leaving the field.

The United States spends about $2,400 per infant through 5-year-old for early education and child care, whereas countries in the European Union spend on average nearly double that at $4,700, and some countries spend three times as much.

"From a business standpoint, I look at this as a long term competitive problem," McBride said. "We don't have a culture of education that exists in some of these other countries. Long-term we're going to face a problem being competitive as a nation."

title: UWA eyes up to 200 students as India campus expansion faces first test
summary:
The Group of Eight university says affordability, mobility and industry links will distinguish its Mumbai and Chennai campuses, but demand and graduate outcomes remain untested.

The post UWA eyes up to 200 students as India campus expansion faces first test appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
The University of Western Australia (UWA) expects to enrol between 100 and 200 students across its Mumbai and Chennai campuses by year-end as it begins testing demand for its degrees in India.

UWA opened its Mumbai campus on September 18, becoming the first member of Australia’s Group of Eight to open a campus in India and marking the university’s first teaching and learning presence outside Australia.

The campus was inaugurated by Western Australian premier Roger Cook and Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis.

“This campus reinforces Mumbai’s position as a global centre for education, business and innovation and gives our young people access to a globally recognised education,” Fadnavis said.

Vice-chancellor Amit Chakma told The PIE News that UWA was beginning with a “relatively small” cohort after receiving final approval for Mumbai only weeks before opening.

At the time of the interview, UWA was awaiting approval for its Chennai campus, which was scheduled to open in October, according to the university, leaving enrolment numbers uncertain despite tentative offers to prospective students.

Although UWA has not promoted the campuses internationally, around 8% of those registering interest are from outside India, representing around a dozen countries in the region, according to Chakma.

He expects the campuses to attract more international students as Australia tightens entry requirements and the cost of studying overseas continues to rise.

Students could complete an undergraduate degree in India, spend time on exchange in Perth and potentially return to Australia for postgraduate study, Chakma said.

“This is a much more affordable option,” he said, adding that students would receive the same standard of education as those studying in Perth.

The comments follow Australia’s announcement of new restrictions on international students, including limits on dependants, tighter course-transfer rules and requirements to progress to higher qualification levels.

TNE helps. To us, where the students study is secondary; what they study is important

Amit Chakma, University of Western Australia

Asked by The PIE whether expanding transnational education (TNE) could help sustain Australia’s international education links while restrictions at home increased, Cook said the state remained strongly supportive of students coming to Australia.

“I’m a humble state premier, so I don’t have control over the rules of migration or visas to Australia,” Cook said.

However, he said the Mumbai campus gave students another route into Australian higher education without requiring them to relocate at that stage of their studies.

Chakma said TNE offered students greater choice based on their visa prospects and financial capacity, while preserving opportunities for mobility in both directions.

“TNE helps. To us, where the students study is secondary; what they study is important,” he said.

UWA plans two-way exchanges between its India and Perth campuses, with Chakma calling six or 12 months in Australia “better than zero” for students unable to study an entire degree overseas.

The model arrives as India’s emerging branch-campus sector faces questions over demand, pricing and graduate outcomes.

Research reported by The PIE identified 13 international universities admitting students across 14 Indian campuses in 2026/27, with a combined annual intake capacity of 2,730.

Rahul Choudaha, author of the report, had said that he expected actual enrolment across the sector to fall below half that capacity, citing late approvals and a wait-and-watch approach among parents seeking evidence on teaching quality, facilities and placements.

Although cheaper than studying overseas, average annual tuition stands at INR 13.3 lakh (£10,400) for undergraduate courses and INR 17.2 lakh (£13,400) for postgraduate courses, with undergraduate fees averaging 115% more than at selected leading Indian private universities.

UWA’s AUD$80 million investment in its wholly owned India campuses has created around 100 direct and 700 wider jobs, according to chancellor Diane Smith-Gander.

The university has also announced 140 scholarships and bursaries, including three full scholarships jointly funded by UWA and the Maharashtra government.

Its 10-year plan anticipates at least 10,000 students across Mumbai and Chennai, although Chakma said UWA would reassess its physical capacity around the halfway point before deciding whether to expand vertically or move to larger premises.

Both campuses will initially offer the same business and technology courses, including computer science, data science, AI, cybersecurity and a 12-month MBA launching in November.

The campuses will become more distinct through their local industry connections rather than substantial differences inside the classroom, Chakma said.

Chennai is expected to develop stronger links with IT, manufacturing and engineering, while Mumbai will lean more heavily towards business.

“The core will remain the same, but the flavour will change,” he said.

UWA is prioritising work-integrated learning, with Chakma saying its India campuses would be more career-focused than undergraduate education in Australia to reflect student expectations and the scale of the country’s industry base.

The university began approaching employers around 18 months before opening. HCLTech will provide students with a free 35-hour AI programme, while Australian data-centre operator AirTrunk has agreed to support internship opportunities.

UWA has also announced an alliance with Larsen & Toubro, while Tata Group and Zoho are among the organisations involved in its wider industry network.

UWA deputy vice-chancellor for global engagement Jennifer Howell said the network would offer internships and placements while allowing employers to contribute to curriculum development.

UWA is also seeking to address concerns that branch campuses could become teaching outposts with limited contributions to Indian research. It has recruited 35 academics through international searches using the same appointment criteria as in Perth, with staff carrying teaching, research and service responsibilities.

Chakma said researchers would work with colleagues in Australia and at Indian institutions, with early projects being explored in agriculture, oceans and medical technology. Sports science is also likely to be considered when UWA seeks approval for its next round of programmes.

For UWA, the immediate test will be converting early interest into enrolments before demonstrating whether its promises around industry experience, mobility and research can justify the price of an international degree in India.

Looking beyond that challenge, Chakma said he was already considering what UWA’s Indian presence could become over the next two decades.

“When we started, it was an idea. Now we are here, but now that we are here, I can see the future,” he said.

title: Small Moves, Big Impact: Building a Positive Climate in Online Classes
summary:
When I think of a positive classroom climate, I picture a brightly lit classroom with students sitting around tables, a soft buzz of student discussion, and the teacher facilitating their learning. But I am old-fashioned. Those days are long gone for many of us who teach online or hybrid courses with asynchronous or synchronous components.  […]

The post Small Moves, Big Impact: Building a Positive Climate in Online Classes appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
When I think of a positive classroom climate, I picture a brightly lit classroom with students sitting around tables, a soft buzz of student discussion, and the teacher facilitating their learning. But I am old-fashioned. Those days are long gone for many of us who teach online or hybrid courses with asynchronous or synchronous components.

One of the challenges that online instructors face is creating a sense of connectedness in which students feel present, “seen,” heard, and part of the learning community. We know student engagement and learning are enhanced when students feel connected—students to the content, students to the instructor, and students to each other. In online environments, social presence is when students perceive that others are real, accessible, and engaged. Researchers such as Garrison (2017) and Lowenthal and Dunlap (2018) have linked increased social presence to higher student satisfaction, stronger participation, and more meaningful learning experiences in online settings. Given this, I offer several strategies to increase social presence and improve your online classroom climate.

First Impressions

The beginning of any course is an essential time for establishing a positive classroom climate. Professors can introduce themselves with a short bio, rather than a professional vita. A photo collage or short video introduction (think Reels on Instagram) can highlight personal and professional experiences and interests that connect you to the content, university, or your students’ experiences.

There are several strategies for students to get to know each other, including posting a text-based introduction, a picture that has meaning for them, or a video introduction. Instructors can use tools within their institution’s learning management system or external tools, such as collaborative documents, to personalize introductions. I teach aspiring school leaders, and some of my favorite introductory prompts are to have students write about their favorite principal or their favorite supervisor. This type of self-disclosure prompt announces to the instructor and their classmates what they value in addition to their background and experiences. It creates a climate that allows students to show their authentic selves and take risks as they begin the course.

Creating Community

Almost 30 years ago, Garrison et al. (1999) wrote that, in online environments, social presence can distinguish a collaborative community of inquiry from a simple process of downloading information. The same is true today, and instructors can use numerous strategies to promote a community of inquiry. One of the most powerful exercises to help people feel connected is to get everyone’s voice in the room. This can happen through a check-in question for synchronous sessions or a discussion prompt for asynchronous courses. These prompts can be personal, such as talking about your favorite animal or superpower, or more related to the course content. Instructors can also use reaction emoticons and thumbs up to help students feel appreciated and valued.

A positive classroom climate is built and sustained when students feel comfortable expressing themselves and offering their unique perspectives. Discussion boards can be a great way to build knowledge by having students post and then respond to their classmates, but sometimes they can hurt authentic connections. A response such as “great idea” can squash connections, as it comes across as transactional and compliance driven. Rather, instructors can encourage and notice more organic and personalized responses.

In Small Teaching Online, Darby and Flowers (2019) remind us, “It’s easy to forget that a name on the screen represents a human being who can benefit from your presence and benefit your learning with their presence” (p. 81). To combat this, instructors can design discussion prompts that encourage debate, allow students to share their perspectives, or discuss a real-life case or scenario without a single, correct answer.

Creating community can be challenging with large groups. Whether through online discussions or breakout rooms in synchronous sessions, smaller groups can enhance students’ social presence and, thus, the classroom climate and learning. I have found that discussion groups of three or four students allow students to be exposed to the ideas of various classmates and enhance student-to-student learning.

In many of my classes, students attend synchronous sessions every other week. After the first session in which everyone introduces themselves, I use breakout rooms once or twice per session. Usually, I let the computer assign the groups so that everyone has a chance to interact with different learners in the class. Then, during the sessions, I give a few extra minutes in the breakout groups so students can reintroduce themselves, have an opportunity to share, and check in with each other about burning issues. Allowing a few extra minutes in breakout rooms lets students share their authentic selves with each other and offer support.

Sustaining Community

In a face-to-face classroom, instructors sustain a positive environment by showing up to class ready and energized. Within a virtual environment, instructors need to check in often and interact in small ways since “too much prolonged silence on our part is a sure way to kill the energy in an online class” (Darby & Flowers, 2019, p. 89). I’ll add that silence can also squash a positive learning environment.

Instructors can use students’ names in their responses, participate in discussions with comments or simple emoticons, and provide timely feedback to let their students know they are present, too. Announcements and short videos are also great ways to connect with students. One of my colleagues introduces each module in her asynchronous classes with a short three-to-five-minute video overview, which her students report helps them feel connected to the class and provides them motivation and inspiration for the week’s learning.

Enhancing a positive learning environment within an online environment only takes small moves: focusing on introductions, allowing for opportunities for real sharing, being present in discussions, and personalizing feedback. It’s never too late to leverage strategies to build connections, community, and a positive climate in your online classes.

Amie Cieminski, EdD, is an associate professor and department chair at the University of Northern Colorado in Greeley, Colorado. Previously, she worked as a teacher, principal, director of professional learning, and school district administrator in several K-12 school districts. Amie teaches educational leadership preparation courses such as the principalship and instructional leadership as well as district level leadership, organizational change, and doctoral research classes for aspiring educational leaders. Her research interests include instructional practices; leadership development; and inclusive, equitable, and socially just leadership.

References

Darby, Flower, and James M. Lang. Small Teaching Online: Applying Learning Science in Online Classes. San Francisco: Jossey-Bass, 2019.

Garrison, D. Randy. E-Learning in the 21st Century: A Community of Inquiry Framework for Research and Practice. 3rd ed. New York: Routledge, 2017.

Garrison, D. Randy, Terry Anderson, and Walter Archer. “Critical Inquiry in a Text-Based Environment: Computer Conferencing in Higher Education.” The Internet and Higher Education 2, nos. 2–3 (1999): 87–105.

title: From Gatekeeper to Waymaker: Reframing Rigor Through Empathy

The post From Gatekeeper to Waymaker: Reframing Rigor Through Empathy appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
Recently, I met with a struggling student who had fallen behind after a series of personal setbacks. Our conversation was practical – we reviewed deadlines, clarified expectations, and outlined next steps. At the end of our meeting, he paused and said, “Your empathy is palpable. In this space, that is rare – and I am grateful.”

I was touched. And without premeditation, I replied, “I did not become an educator to be a gatekeeper; I became an educator to be a waymaker.”

The statement lingered with me long after the meeting ended.

Higher education has long been shaped by a gatekeeping narrative. Faculty are positioned as protectors of standards, arbiters of readiness, and guardians of disciplinary rigor. In some contexts, this role is framed as necessary to maintain academic quality. Yet too often gatekeeping drifts into something else: ambiguity mistaken for rigor, distance mistaken for professionalism, and difficulty mistaken for depth.

But what if rigor and empathy are not opposites? What if our role is not to guard the threshold, but to design the path forward?

The Limits of the Gatekeeping Paradigm

Research on student persistence suggests that belonging matters as much as preparation. Vincent Tinto argues that students persist when they feel academically and socially integrated into their institutions. When students perceive themselves as outsiders to academic culture, withdrawal becomes more likely.

Similarly, research by Gregory Walton and Geoffrey Cohen on belonging uncertainty shows that students from marginalized or nontraditional backgrounds may interpret ordinary academic struggle as evidence that they do not belong. Small signals from instructors – tone, feedback, and clarity of expectations – can either exacerbate or reduce that uncertainty.

Gatekeeping, when enacted rigidly, can unintentionally amplify belonging uncertainty. Waymaking, by contrast, clarifies the path without lowering the bar.

Waymaking Is Not Leniency

To be a waymaker does not mean reducing standards or inflating grades. Waymaking provides transparency, scaffolds complexity, and preserves dignity while maintaining intellectual challenge. Essentially, waymaking creates avenues toward student success.

Research on transparent assignment design, led by Mary-Ann Winkelmes, demonstrates that when faculty clearly articulate the purpose, task, and criteria of assignments, student performance improves – particularly for first-generation and historically underserved students. Transparency does not dilute rigor; it enhances access to it. Likewise, John Hattie’s synthesis of research on feedback underscores that timely, specific, growth-oriented feedback has one of the strongest impacts on student achievement. Students improve not when we guard standards, but when we illuminate how to meet them.

Rigor is about cognitive demand, not obscurity. Waymaking asks:

Have I clearly articulated what high-quality work looks like?

Have I modeled the thinking process required?

Have I provided opportunities for practice before high-stakes evaluation?

Have I distinguished between cognitive rigor and facilitative rigidity?

Have I created multiple and diverse pathways for achievement?

Practical Shifts Toward Waymaking

Shifting from gatekeeper to waymaker requires neither a full paradigm shift nor a complete course redesign. It begins with small but intentional changes.

1. Making the invisible visible.

Narrate your thinking. Provide exemplars. Offer transparency in assessment by making rubrics and guides available. Externalize the tacit knowledge that experts carry implicitly. This scaffolding reduces academic mystique and gives students a clear understanding of expectations.

2. Normalize “not yet.”

Language shapes motivation. Carol Dweck’s work on growth mindset reminds us that framing ability as developable increases persistence. When feedback signals progress rather than deficiency, students are more likely to revise and reengage.

3. Use structured flexibility.

Clear policies paired with humane discretion communicate both standards and care. Exercising judgment does not weaken expectations; it reinforces professional discernment.

4. Build early mastery experiences.

According to Albert Bandura, self-efficacy develops through skill acquisition that leads to performance accomplishments. Low-stakes assessments early in a course allow students to calibrate their understanding before major evaluations, strengthening both competence and confidence.

These practices align with research on belonging, motivation, and self-efficacy. Students are more likely to engage deeply when they perceive both challenge and support.

Reframing Rigor

There is a persistent myth in higher education that compassion weakens standards. In practice, the opposite is often true. When expectations are unclear, students expend cognitive energy decoding assignments rather than engaging content. When feedback feels punitive, students protect their ego instead of revising their work. When policies are rigid without explanation, students may interpret struggle as exclusion rather than growth.

Waymaking reduces unnecessary friction so that intellectual effort can be directed where it belongs: analysis, synthesis, and application. Rigor, properly understood, involves sustained cognitive challenge supported by clear structure. This encourages depth of thinking while eliminating unnecessary obstacles.

A Professional Responsibility

Empathy in education is sometimes framed as a personality trait. I would argue it is a professional responsibility. Empathy does not require agreement with every request or the removal of every consequence. It requires perspective-taking. It asks us to consider what students can reasonably know, given their prior experiences, and how our design choices either widen or narrow access to success. When students say that empathy feels rare, that should give us pause.

Instructors operate under increasing pressure – large enrollments, institutional constraints, and workload strain. Gatekeeping can feel efficient. After all, it is faster to enforce a rule than to explain it, and easier to default to policy than to exercise judgment. But efficiency is not the same as effectiveness. If our aim is authentic learning, academic persistence, and intellectual development, then our task is not merely to sort students into categories of capable and incapable. Our task is to cultivate capability. That is the work of a waymaker.

At the end of that meeting, the student left with a plan – not a pass. He still had deadlines to meet, standards to satisfy, and work to complete. But he also left with clarity, dignity, and the belief that the path forward was visible. We cannot eliminate all barriers our students face. But within our courses, we can decide whether we stand at the threshold or walk alongside our students on the path. We can guard the gate – or we can make a way.

Crystal Donlan, MEd, DEd, is the Associate Director of Digital Pedagogy & Scholarship at Bucknell University, a long-standing adjunct professor at Luzerne County Community College, and a doctoral candidate in Learning and Performance Systems at Penn State University. A learning scientist and lifelong educator, her work focuses on distance learning, modern literacies, and human-centered practices toward belonging, persistence, and meaning.

References

Bandura, A. (1997). Self-efficacy: The exercise of control. Freeman.

Dweck, C. S. (2006). Mindset: The new psychology of success. Random House.

Hattie, J. (2009). Visible learning: A synthesis of over 800 meta-analyses relating to achievement. Routledge.

Tinto, V. (2012). Completing college: Rethinking institutional action. University of Chicago Press.

Walton, G. M., & Cohen, G. L. (2011). A brief social-belonging intervention improves academic and health outcomes. Science, 331(6023), 1447–1451.

Winkelmes, M.-A., Bernacki, M., Butler, J., Zochowski, M., Golanics, J., & Harriss Weavil, K. (2016). A teaching intervention that increases underserved college students’ success. Peer Review, 18(1/2).

title: Why students attend: moving from monitoring absence towards understanding engagement
summary: The post Why students attend: moving from monitoring absence towards understanding engagement appeared first on Advance HE UK.
full_text:
Michael Lupton, Steph Sayan, Jennifer Schevchenko, Nicola Cutting and Lauren McSorley discuss their research into falling student attendance rates across HE institutions.

Student attendance is one of the most closely monitored indicators of participation in Higher Education, routinely linked to academic achievement and retention and used as a proxy for engagement. But while these systems tell us who attends and when, they cannot tell us why. Understanding these motivations lets us move beyond monitoring absence, towards strategies that actively motivate engagement.

To explore this, we held focus groups with undergraduate BSc Psychology students at Hull and York St John, analysed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2022). Participants rarely described attendance as a straightforward decision based on motivation. Instead, it was shaped by interconnected factors — teaching practices, timetabling, social relationships, personal circumstances, institutional support — the consequence of wider experiences, not a simple yes/no choice.

This aligns with broader research: attendance is often treated as a static metric, but engagement is broader — students’ academic, social and emotional connections to their learning environment (Krause & Coates, 2008), reciprocally shaped by effort from both students and educators (Trowler, 2010). Attendance may indicate engagement, but it is not engagement itself. Rather than asking why students don’t attend, we asked what makes attendance worthwhile. Four themes were constructed: the learning experience, the role of lecturers, the practical realities of university life, and a sense of belonging.

Students do not simply attend lectures — they attend learning experiences

Students described struggling to concentrate during two-hour lectures built around one-way delivery: “when it’s just the lecturer talking for 2 hours straight, it’s hard to keep focussed.”

By contrast, students valued active participation. Interactive approaches — Mentimeter, discussion, debate, collaborative activities — made sessions more engaging: “It makes it less about the lecturer talking at you for two hours and more of you actually understand what they’re saying because you’re involved in it.” This matches research linking attendance to classes perceived as valuable and stimulating (Kelly, 2012; Moores et al., 2019), through activities connecting students with ideas and communities (Krause, 2005). Students weren’t asking for easier content — even on less interesting topics, interactivity increased willingness to attend. They were rejecting passivity, not challenge.

Lecturer enthusiasm strongly shaped willingness to attend: “If they’re genuinely excited about it, then you kind of get engaged with it.” Conversely, students avoided sessions offering little beyond the slides: “I’ve not learnt any more from you than I could have done reading this at home.” This mirrors research linking attendance to engaging, enthusiastic teaching that offers more than independently accessible material (Lang et al., 2007; Kelly, 2012; Sloan et al., 2020).

Students attend people, not PowerPoint slides

Teaching styles also suit people differently, and students sometimes chose sessions accordingly. Feeling comfortable mattered too — one participant described a lecturer’s comment about lateness leading a student to avoid future sessions altogether. Attendance decisions aren’t always about content, but about whether students feel respected and welcomed in the learning environment.

The timetable is part of the learning environment

Where lecturers often focus on what happens inside a session, participants highlighted factors long before it begins: “The timetable can be a bit of a nightmare.” They described long gaps between sessions, difficulty establishing routines, and issues with travelling to campus for a single lecture at “awkward times.”

Timetabling, travel and commuting pressures are established influences on attendance (Lang et al., 2007; Kelly, 2012; Sloan et al., 2020). Tellingly, staff often frame attendance as motivational, while students describe it as logistical. Institutions shape the conditions that make participation easier or harder (Krause & Coates, 2008; Trowler, 2010); the timetable is part of the learning environment, not just a schedule.

Fostering a sense of belonging can be a meaningful attendance intervention

Social relationships strongly influenced attendance. One participant put it bluntly: “I’ve got no mates in my lecture — why do I have to go?” This points to something real: learning is fundamentally social, and students engage more when they feel part of a community (Krause, 2005; Krause & Coates, 2008). Having friends on the course encouraged attendance; when friends left early or skipped sessions, others often followed.

Several participants felt they hadn’t had enough opportunity to build relationships in first year, suggesting informal study groups and more chances to interact beyond existing friendship circles. Institutions may do better by creating socially connected environments than by monitoring or enforcing attendance.

Attendance data tells us who is absent, but rarely why

These findings raise a further question: what can attendance data actually show? Today’s students juggle competing demands — part-time work, caring responsibilities, long commutes. A 2023 survey found 49% of respondents had missed a class for paid employment (Johnson, 2023); participants also cited childcare, transport disruption, financial pressure, family difficulties and mental health challenges.

Attendance is shaped by both institutional and individual factors and rarely explained by a single one (Moores et al., 2019; Sloan et al., 2020). Two students with identical records may have entirely different reasons for missing classes — one disengaged, another managing real difficulty while remaining committed. Attendance data is a starting point for dialogue, not a definitive measure of engagement, and a prompt to ask whether support systems match students’ realities.

Looking beyond attendance

Attendance is better understood as a consequence of broader educational, social and personal factors than as an outcome in itself. Participants attended when sessions were engaging, lecturers enthusiastic, timetables manageable, they felt connected to others, and life circumstances allowed it; lower attendance more often reflected a mix of these factors than a simple lack of motivation.

Perhaps the question is not “How do we make students attend?” but “How do we design learning opportunities students do not want to miss?” None of these factors alone guarantees attendance, but together they create the conditions for engagement to develop.

Key takeaways:

Prioritise interactive teaching over passive delivery.

Make space to build students’ sense of belonging and social connection into teaching time.

Treat attendance data as a starting point for dialogue, not a verdict on motivation.

These findings shift attendance work away from compliance and towards educational design, community and student support — less monitoring of presence, more creating environments in which students feel able, connected, and motivated to participate.

References

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2022). Conceptual and design thinking for thematic analysis. Qualitative Psychology, 9(1), 3–26. https://doi.org/10.1037/qup0000196

Johnson K. (2023, March 6). Cost of living: ‘I skip university lectures to do paid work instead’. BBC News. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/newsbeat-64816948

Kelly, G. E. (2012). Lecture attendance rates at university and related factors. Journal of Further and Higher Education, 36(1), 17–40. https://doi.org/10.1080/0309877X.2011.596196

Krause, K. L. (2005). Understanding and promoting student engagement in university learning communities. Paper presented as keynote address: Engaged, Inert or Otherwise Occupied, 21-22.

Krause, K. L., & Coates, H. (2008). Students’ engagement in first-year university. Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, 33(5), 493–505. https://doi.org/10.1080/02602930701698892

Lang, M., Joyce, A., Conaty, F., & Kelly, B. (2008). An analysis of factors influencing the attendance of first year university students.

Moores, E., Birdi, G. K., & Higson, H. E. (2019). Determinants of university students’ attendance. Educational Research, 61(4), 371–387. https://doi.org/10.1080/00131881.2019.1660587

Sloan, D., Manns, H., Mellor, A., & Jeffries, M. (2020). Factors influencing student non-attendance at formal teaching sessions. Studies in Higher Education, 45(11), 2203–2216. https://doi.org/10.1080/03075079.2019.1599849

title: Flexible Lehre – Ein Update für mehr soziale Präsenz
summary:
Wie lernen Studierende am besten? Warum bedeutet physische Anwesenheit nicht automatisch soziale Präsenz? Und wie können Lernformate so gestaltet werden, dass sie in der Balance zwischen Präsenz und Online allen gerecht werden? Der Beitrag von Nicole Vögele ist der siebte Teil unserer Reihe „Paartherapie für Hochschulen“. Darin untersuchen DigitalChangeMaker gemeinsam, wie Hochschulen und Studierende wieder stärker miteinander ins Gespräch kommen können, um Lehren und Lernen zukunftsfähig zu gestalten.

The post Flexible Lehre – Ein Update für mehr soziale Präsenz appeared first on Hochschulforum Digitalisierung.
full_text:
In den bisherigen Blogbeiträgen haben wir uns unter anderem mit den unterschiedlichen Lebensrealitäten von Student:innen sowie dem Mehrwert von Präsenzlehre beschäftigt. Student:innen balancieren Haushalt, Erwerbsarbeit und Privatleben, während der klassische Studienplan oft verlangt, vor Ort Wissen aufzunehmen, es zu Hause zu vertiefen und in der Prüfungsphase wieder auszuschütten. Doch „Präsenz“ muss nicht rein physisch definiert sein.

Echte Anwesenheit bedeutet mehr, als nur im Raum zu sitzen: Es bedeutet, aktiv teilzunehmen, Fragen zu stellen und über das vermittelte Wissen hinauszudenken. Um dieses kognitive Lernen in vollumfänglicher Präsenz zu ermöglichen und die gemeinsame Zeit auf dem Campus wertvoll zu gestalten, ist es wichtig, flexible Strukturen und Lehrformate zu implementieren.

Studierende haben sich ihre dynamischen Lebensrealitäten nicht freiwillig ausgesucht. Oft sind es schlichtweg strukturelle Konsequenzen, die ein Studium heutzutage mit sich bringt. Wer hohe Mietpreise in Campusnähe umgehen muss, nimmt lange Pendelwege in Kauf. Wer Semesterbeiträge, Miete und Lebensunterhalt finanzieren muss, geht nebenbei arbeiten (wie schon im Blogbeitrag zu Lebensrealitäten aufgezeigt).

Diese beiden Realitäten prallen im Hochschulalltag oft aufeinander. Modulhandbücher und Curricula orientieren sich traditionell primär an inhaltlichen Vorgaben und viel zu selten an der zeitlichen oder organisatorischen Durchführbarkeit für eine diverse Studierendenschaft.

Gleichzeitig wächst die Menge an vermitteltem Wissen rasant. Gerade in anwendungsorientierten Disziplinen wie MINT verdichtet sich der Stoff enorm, während das Zeitbudget starr bei vier bis sechs Semesterwochenstunden (SWS) pro Modul bei Studierenden und acht bis 18 SWS bei Professuren (von Düring, 2026) bleibt. Durch das anwachsende Wissen in Verbindung mit dem Mangel an eingeräumter Zeit zur Vermittlung dessen kann ein Overload entstehen, bei dem Abstriche gemacht werden müssen, weil die reine Zeit für die Inhaltsvermittlung im Seminarraum schlicht nicht mehr ausreicht. An diesem Punkt wird deutlich, dass der traditionelle Frontalunterricht als gängigste Lehrmethode an seine Grenzen stößt. Insbesondere Fachhochschulen bzw. Hochschulen für Angewandte Wissenschaften (HAW) zeichnen sich ihrem institutionellen Profil nach durch eine starke Praxis- und Anwendungsorientierung aus, während Universitäten traditionell stärker forschungsorientiert sind (Hochschulkompass, 2022). Wenn die kostbare Präsenzzeit jedoch primär dafür genutzt wird, deklaratives Wissen in einer Einweg-Kommunikation zu „senden“, geht genau dieser Anwendungsbezug verloren.

Der Fokus muss zwingend auf der Vertiefung und dem Transfer des Wissens liegen, nicht auf dem bloßen Diktieren von Fakten. Obwohl Lehrende durch die Freiheit der Lehre durchaus den Gestaltungsspielraum haben, die Art der Inhaltsvermittlung agil an die Bedürfnisse der Student:innen, sowie den Ansprüchen an Lernfortschritte und zeitgemäßer Lehre anzupassen, wird dieses Potenzial im Lehralltag noch zu selten konsequent durch ergänzende Formate ausgeschöpft (Budde & Friedrich, 2024). Wenn die Freiheit der Lehre nicht mit den passenden strukturellen Mitteln, wie Schulungen, Problembewusstsein und Kapazitäten ergänzt wird, kann auch kein Fortschritt entstehen. Hier muss ein Umdenken stattfinden: und genau hier kommt die flexible Lehre ins Spiel.

Flexible Lehre meint im Kern, den Lernenden bewusste Wahlmöglichkeiten und Autonomie hinsichtlich Zeit, Ort und Lerntempo einzuräumen, um Lernbarrieren abzubauen (Collis & Moonen, 2001). Lerntempo bedeutet hier nicht nur das Tempo innerhalb eines Moduls, sondern für den ganzen Studienverlauf. Deswegen könnte man auch behaupten, dass Flexibilisierung auch bedeutet, den Rahmen der Regelstudienzeit, und somit übergeordnet des Vollzeitstudiums aufbrechen zu können.

Ein Blick über den Tellerrand lohnt sich: Fernhochschulen haben jahrelange Erfahrung damit, wie Wissen didaktisch so aufbereitet wird, dass Studierende es sich asynchron und ortsunabhängig aneignen können. Dies wird auch bei Studierenden deutlich: “Der private Hochschulsektor hat sich in den vergangenen Jahren sehr dynamisch entwickelt – insbesondere im Hinblick auf die Studierendenzahlen, die sich zwischen 2015 und 2024 nahezu verdoppelt haben.
